authorization.name: join with blanket .*::.*
authorization.why: M11 decision 5 assumed a blanket grant authorizes everything. Upstream refuses it: the claim is matched against JOIN::<room>, and `.*::.*` requires a `::` the room name does not have.

authorization.name: join with blanket .*
authorization.why: The other shape of a blanket grant, refused for the same reason. Paired with the acceptances below so the refusals cannot be explained by a server that refuses every join.

authorization.name: join with JOIN::.*
authorization.why: The acceptance that makes the two refusals above mean something: an explicit JOIN verb is what upstream requires.

authorization.name: join with JOIN::<this room>
authorization.why: An exact-room grant is honoured, so the verb is matched per room and not merely present.

authorization.name: join with JOIN::<other room>
authorization.why: The paired refusal for the row above: same verb, wrong room. Together they show the room name is really being matched.

authorization.name: watch data_trigger with WATCH::.*
authorization.why: A data trigger is authorized by the WATCH verb, as expected.

authorization.name: watch device_trigger, device_id inside simple_trigger
authorization.why: A device trigger is authorized only when simple_trigger carries device_id itself.

authorization.name: watch device_trigger, device_id only at payload top level
authorization.why: The paired refusal: identical except that device_id sits where the AppEngine REST API puts it. Upstream calls this `unauthorized`, which is a misleading reason for a payload-shape problem — a client author would look at their token.

authorization.name: watch device_trigger for device_id "*"
authorization.why: A wildcard device is refused even under WATCH::.*, so device triggers cannot be watched realm-wide from a room.

authorization.name: watch data_trigger, claim WATCH::<device>/<interface> (Astrate's shape)
authorization.why: Astrate authorizes a data trigger against `<device_id>/<interface>`, with no match path. If upstream built the same string this is accepted; if upstream appends the match path it is refused, because the anchored claim regex cannot match the longer string.

authorization.name: watch data_trigger, claim WATCH::<device>/<interface><match_path>
authorization.why: The paired alternative, and upstream's shape according to its source (`"#{device_id}/#{interface_name}#{path}"`, with no separator because the path already starts with a slash). Exactly one of this row and the one above can be accepted, so together they identify the authorization path rather than merely confirming a guess.

authorization.name: watch device_trigger, claim WATCH::<this device>
authorization.why: A device trigger's authorization path is claimed to be the bare device id. A narrow, exact claim accepts it, which is what identifies the path.

authorization.name: watch device_trigger, claim WATCH::<another device>
authorization.why: The paired refusal for the row above: a well-formed claim naming a different device. Together they show the device id is really the string being matched, rather than the acceptance coming from any claim at all.

authorization.name: watch group data_trigger (group_name top level), claim WATCH::groups/<group>/<interface><match_path>
authorization.why: Astrate's predicted shape. If upstream builds the same authorization path for a group trigger this is accepted.

authorization.name: watch group data_trigger, claim WATCH::groups/<group>/<interface> (no match path)
authorization.why: The paired refusal for the row above, mirroring what the device-shape recording found: without the match path appended the anchored claim cannot match.

authorization.name: watch group data_trigger, claim WATCH::<device>/<interface><match_path> (the device shape)
authorization.why: The alternative reading: that a group trigger authorizes against the publishing device's path. Exactly one of this row and the first group row can be accepted, so together they identify which string upstream builds.

authorization.name: watch group data_trigger (group_name inside simple_trigger), claim WATCH::groups/<group>/<interface><match_path>
authorization.why: The other payload shape a client might send: group_name nested where Astrate reads it. If upstream refuses this one with a validation error rather than an authorization refusal, the field belongs at the top level only.
authorization.reply: ["1","2","rooms:bench:probe","phx_reply",{"status":"error","response":{"errors":{"group_name":["must be present if device_id is not set"],"device_id":["must be present if group_name is not set"]}}}]

authorization.name: watch group device_trigger (device_id "*" inside simple_trigger), claim WATCH::groups/<group>
authorization.why: Astrate's predicted shape for a group device trigger: the bare group name. The payload needs device_id="*" inside simple_trigger — a concrete id is refused with reason "device_id must be * for group triggers", the mirror image of plain device triggers where "*" is refused.

authorization.name: watch group device_trigger, claim WATCH::groups/<other group>
authorization.why: The paired refusal: same verb, wrong group name, so the group name is really being matched.

device_errors.name: valid publish
device_errors.why: The acceptance row. Without it, a stack that emitted device_error for everything would satisfy every row below.

device_errors.name: interface not in introspection
device_errors.why: Astrate maps its own interface_not_in_introspection to invalid_interface. This row is what upstream actually says.

device_errors.name: unknown path on a known interface
payload that is not BSON at all
string where the mapping says double
BSON document with no v key
valid publish on a device-owned interface (extended introspection)
device_errors.why: The acceptance row for this section: same extended introspection as every row below, no error. Without it a stack that errored on everything would satisfy every rejection row.

device_errors.name: publish on a server-owned interface
device_errors.why: Issue #18. The interface is in the device's introspection, so the rejection cannot be interface_loading_failed; Astrate maps its ownership_violation to write_on_server_owned_interface. This row is what upstream actually says.

device_errors.name: largest payload observed delivered end-to-end
device_errors.why: Issue #19's lower bound, measured by bisection: a 65468-byte BSON document (MQTT packet just under 64 KiB) is stored and queryable. Recorded as an observation, not a guarantee — the exact bound belongs to the transcript.

device_errors.name: payload one step past the packet cap
device_errors.why: Issue #19's upper bound: a 65473-byte BSON document pushes the MQTT packet over 65536 bytes. Upstream ACKs the publish and then silently drops it — no storage, no device_error, no session change. Astrate instead rejects such payloads itself and emits value_size_exceeded; this row records that upstream, on this surface, says nothing at all.

device_errors.name: string well above the type limit
device_errors.why: astarte_core validates strings > 65536 bytes as value_size_exceeded, but a publish that size can never reach that validator over MQTT — the packet cap drops it first. Three attempts recorded whether any device_error escapes anyway.
